analysis.one_liner: Charges miners small fees and a 3% royalty to mine public land, while letting them buy that land cheaply.
analysis.headline: The Mining Law Reform Act of 1995, a mining-industry-shaped rewrite of the 1872 law, was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, held one subcommittee hearing, and never received a vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under an 1872 law, mining companies could take gold, silver, and other hardrock minerals from federal land without paying royalties, and could patent — buy outright — that land for as little as a few dollars an acre. S. 506 would have replaced the old claim-staking system with flat fees and a 3% royalty on mining profits, required companies to post bonds for cleanup, and created an abandoned-mine reclamation fund. But it also repealed the moratorium on new land patents and defined reclamation mostly by state standards, terms shaped by the mining industry it regulated. It never left committee and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Mining companies operating on federal land. They would gain a predictable, low-cost system: a flat $100-per-claim fee, a 3% royalty on net proceeds with generous deductions, waivers for small operators, reclamation standards keyed to state law, patents at fair market value of the surface (not the minerals), and new statutory property rights in claims. States with mining interests would also receive shares of royalties and reclamation money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

how_it_helps.text: It replaced the 1872 system's patchwork with a flat $100-per-claim annual maintenance fee and a $25 location fee, replacing the 1993 fees and the old annual assessment-work requirements.

It imposed a 3% royalty on the net proceeds of minerals from federal claims — the first time hardrock mining on federal land would pay any production royalty — while waiving it for mines with under $500,000 in annual gross yield.

It required operators to file plans of operations, post financial assurance (bonds) covering reclamation costs, and reclaim disturbed federal land, with an abandoned-mine reclamation program funded by a third of royalty receipts.
It declared that mining claims and patented land could not be diverted to other uses, allowing the land to revert to the United States if a patent was used for anything but good-faith mining.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who own the minerals on federal land: the bill would have let companies buy public land at surface value and pay a 3% royalty on profits after deductions — a fraction of the value of publicly owned minerals — and would have limited federal environmental oversight of mining on federal land in favor of state standards. Anyone living downstream or downhill of a mine bears the pollution risk the weaker standards leave behind.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers who own the public minerals

drawbacks.text: The 3% royalty applied only to 'net proceeds' after a long list of deductions — including reclamation, permitting, insurance, and taxes — leaving the government a small slice of the value of minerals taken from public land, far below the rates oil, gas, and coal pay.

It repealed the 1993 claim maintenance fees and the congressional moratorium on processing new patents, reopening the door for mining companies to buy public land outright at the value of the surface alone, with the mineral value excluded from the price.

Reclamation standards would be tailored to state requirements rather than set by federal environmental standards, and a plan compliant with state rules was deemed sufficient to prevent degradation — meaning protection varied by state and mining-heavy states set the bar for their own dominant industry.

It handed mining companies strong new property rights — exclusive possession of claims without physical occupation — and framed the bill's own purpose as avoiding Fifth Amendment takings claims, a provision valued by claimholders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's few public benefits — an end to free mining, a modest royalty, financial assurance for cleanup — were outweighed by its design: the royalty was low and riddled with deductions, the patent path let miners convert public land to private land cheaply, and reclamation standards were set by the states whose economies depend on mining. Critics of the 1872 law argued even these mild terms were unnecessary; supporters of stronger reform (like the House-passed bills of the era) called royalties of this size a continuation of the giveaway. As drafted, the main beneficiary was clearly the mining industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, referred to its Forests and Public Lands Subcommittee, which held one hearing — and that is the last thing that ever happened to it.

narrative.text: Introduced March 7, 1995 by Senator Larry Craig with 14 cosponsors, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
Eight days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Forests and Public Lands, which held a hearing on March 30, 1995.
No further action was taken: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
Had it passed, it would have repealed the 1993 claim maintenance fees and the congressional moratorium on processing new mining patents.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies with claims on federal land, who kept paying no royalty and kept the right to buy public land at 1872 prices. Taxpayers and western lands were spared neither a giveaway nor a cleanup, since no reform of any kind passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining companies; the status quo continued

sides.party_line_note: The 14 cosponsors split 12 Republicans and 2 Democrats, and both Democrats were from Nevada, a mining state; the bill died in committee without a vote, so no roll-call ever showed the chamber's position.

industries.note: The bill ended the 1993 claim fees, replaced them with a lower $100 flat fee, imposed only a 3% net-proceeds royalty with extensive deductions, and reopened cheap patenting of federal land. Its stated purposes included promoting mineral development and avoiding takings claims against the government.

industries.industry: Mine reclamation contractors and bonding/insurance providers
industries.note: Financial assurance and reclamation requirements would create a market for bonds and reclamation work, though this was incidental to the bill's main thrust.

States could take over administration of mining regulation through cooperative agreements, share one-third of royalty receipts, and receive abandoned-mine reclamation funds — gaining control and revenue while absorbing regulatory work.
